_comment: THE BOUNDARY RULE, AS DATA, BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN TWICE AND NOTHING COMPARED THE COPIES.
Two suites assert who may know about the identifier-encoding seam, deliberately, because
they run in different recipes: `tests/tidentifierencoding.nim` is in `just test`, which
takes about 37 minutes, and `tools/chain/identifier-encoding-selftest.mjs` is in
`just chain-selftest`, the fast gate people actually run. A boundary that only the slow
gate knew about would be a boundary nobody saw move.
── WHY THE RULE IS HERE AND NOT IN EITHER OF THEM ────────────────────────────────────
Because it was in BOTH of them. The source extensions, the pruned directory names, the
per-directory population floors and the allowlists were spelled out twice and compared to
nothing, and the two halves agreed only because two independently-maintained copies
happened to match. That is not a property, it is a coincidence with a maintenance cost,
and it had already broken once: the Nim half pruned `dist/` with an unanchored
`contains("dist/")` while the JavaScript half pruned by exact directory NAME, so a single
`client/src/redist/x.mjs` put the two populations at 102 and 103. That was found by hand
and fixed by hand, which is exactly the failure mode a single source removes.
So the rule is one file that both halves read, for the reason `identifier-encodings.json`,
`refusal-reasons.json` and `snapshot-format.json` beside it are data: a rule that has to
hold in two languages cannot live in one of them.
── AND THE RULE BEING SHARED IS NOT ENOUGH, WHICH IS THE SECOND HALF ─────────────────
The `redist/` divergence was NOT a disagreement about the rule. Both halves already agreed
that `dist/` is pruned; they disagreed about what `dist/` MEANS, in their own sweep code,
in two languages. Moving the words here would not have caught it.
So the Nim half additionally runs the JavaScript half with `--emit-population` and requires
the two swept file LISTS to be identical, per top-level directory, as sets. That is a check
on the two IMPLEMENTATIONS rather than on the two configurations, and it is the one that
bites on a prune, a glob or a git-population rule that two languages read differently.
Each sweep names the TOKENS whose appearance in a source file makes that file a consumer
of one half of the seam, and enumerates exactly which files may name them. The comparison
is an EQUALITY against a sweep of the whole tree, not a subset check: an unexpected
consumer fails it in one direction and an expected consumer that stopped being one fails
it in the other. The `count` beside each expected list is asserted too, so the list cannot
drift upward one entry at a time with the equality quietly edited to match — a number is a
thing a reviewer sees move.
declaration  who reads `chains[<slug>].identifierEncoding`, the registry member that
says how a chain writes its identifiers. NAMING ALONE WAS MEASURED
LEAKING, which is why the equality is against a sweep: consumers planted
one file over from two named files (`client/src/viewmodel/chain_vm.nim`
beside `chain_registry_vm.nim`, `tools/capture/lib/provenance.mjs` beside
`entities.mjs`) once left every arm green while a universal claim printed.
caseRule     who reads the PER-ENCODING CASE RULE — `identifierKeyForm`,
`identifierDisplayForm`, `identifierPayload`. These are a separate sweep
rather than more tokens on the first one because they are a separate
fact: a file may key an identifier without ever reading a registry row
(the §5 hash index does, under a named global encoding), and a file may
read the row without keying anything (the session pins it). Folding them
together would let one seam's new consumer be excused by the other's
allowlist.
A sweep that found nothing would satisfy every equality above perfectly, because an empty
set equals an empty set. So each top-level directory carries a FLOOR on the number of
source files swept, per directory, so an emptied sweep of one cannot hide behind another.
The floors are the contract; the COUNT is an observation each run prints. Both halves take
their population from git — tracked plus untracked-and-not-ignored — so it moves with the
working tree, and a number pinned here would go stale for anyone holding a scratch file.
(The Justfile header once pinned one and was stale within a day.)
`.gitignore` is where 'this is generated' is already written down, and it is kept current
by whoever adds the recipe. A same-stem heuristic — a `.js` beside a `.nim` of the same
name is `nim js` output — was tried, was measured against the one case it hit
(`client/tests/test_searchboot.js`), and walked straight past `client/Justfile`'s
`search-bundle`, which compiles `searchboot/searchboot.nim` to `searchboot/search.js`:
different stem, so `search.js` was swept as source and reddened the client equality for
anyone who had ever built the bundle, while a clean checkout and CI never saw it. A gate
green where it is checked and red where it is used is worse than one that is merely wrong.
Tracked PLUS untracked-and-not-ignored is the population: the second half is what catches
a consumer that has been written and not yet committed, which is when catching it is most
useful. `ci/test/client-sdk-boundary.sh` derives its population the same way.
── AND THE SWEEPS MATCH OVER CODE, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THE REVERSE DIRECTION LIVE ────
The equality is advertised in both directions, and one of them used to be decoration. The
sweeps matched their tokens over the WHOLE FILE while `pins` matched over CODE, so an
expected consumer that STOPPED being one still matched as long as a doc comment somewhere
in it named the token. MEASURED: that was true of 14 of the 22 expected entries, including
`shards.nim`, `hashshard.nim`, `paths.nim` and `search_shapes.nim`. The proof is a real
revert: `client/src/viewmodel/search_shapes.nim` put back to its own unconditional
`toLowerAscii` has nought code occurrences of all three `caseRule` tokens and one in a doc
comment, and BOTH halves stayed green — and no behavioural test catches it either, because
for lowercase hex the revert is byte-equivalent. Deleting the comment's mention as well
reddened both halves, which is what proves the comment was what saved it.
Both halves now run the sweep through the same `codeOf` filter the pins use.
ONE ENTRY LEFT THE `declaration` SET WHEN THAT LANDED, and it is recorded rather than
quietly dropped: `src/blocktracer_client_paths.nim` had nought code occurrences and one in
a comment. That module is two lines — `import blocktracer_client/paths` and `export paths`
— under a sixty-line header explaining the browser-compilable entry point, and its single
mention of the member is in that header. It is DOCUMENTATION of
`blocktracer_client/paths.nim`'s signature, not a second reader of the declaration, and the
module it re-exports is itself in the set — so a consumer reading the declaration 'through'
it is reading a file the sweep already covers. If it ever grows code that reads the member,
the forward direction reddens on it as an unexpected consumer. `declaration`/`src` is
therefore 8 and not 9.
A boundary check that only watched the CLOSED half of the seam would report the seam shut.
`pins` states what is still hex-shaped and what must no longer be there, as counts over
CODE rather than over comments — counted over comments, a paragraph explaining a defect
reads as the defect. Each pin is expected to go red in its turn, at which point whoever
moved it reads the reason recorded beside it.

sweeps.why: who reads the registry member that says how a chain writes its identifiers

src.why: joined this set when the index stopped being hex-only: it reads the shard rule back through `identifierEncodingRule` to reconstruct a format-1 entry's `0x`, which format 1 physically cannot store
builds, validates and reads it, over the closed set
the ONE derivation, which takes the token as a parameter, and the six identifier-keyed path builders that derive both segments of a path from it
reads the declaration out of the tree it is validating
hands the session's declaration to the paths
the SDK's path facade, which re-exports the builders and the vocabulary their signatures are written in
pins the chain's declaration like the generation

client.why: the browser's search bootstrap, which recomputes the producer's path in a tab

`staticRoutes` places identifiers in ROUTES, which are key positions, while the lists it reads them from are object BODIES carrying display forms — so it needs the chain's declaration to key-form them
the global index's one writer: it reads each chain's declaration back out of the tree it is exporting, so the index is keyed by what the producer published rather than by what this file assumes

reads the ENCODING SET rather than a chain's row, and that is the point: §5's index path has no chain segment, so the browser derives an index key from the query's SHAPE — `identifierEncodingsMatching` over the shared file's `shapes` rule — with no registry in hand at all

tools.why: the JavaScript half's selftest, and still nothing else: the capture tooling enumerates what was published rather than deriving it

§5.2b's census check. It joined this set when §5.6's declaration became reachable: the member is now in the census, so this suite names it, and its §15 asserts the STRUCTURE of the reader's one binding — that `ingest.nim` builds one declaration, publishes that value and keys every path from it. That is a claim about the reader's source which no behavioural test can make, and it derives nothing

sweeps.why: who reads the per-encoding CASE rule — the step that replaced one global toLowerAscii

src.why: reads the `case` rule out of the shared file and answers over it

folds per encoding before it slices, so a shard key is recomputable from either spelling — and names every path object by the same key form, which is what stops a producer writing a folded shard beside a raw name
the §5 index's shard key and format 1's payload, both through `identifierPayload` — so the index and the object tree cannot disagree about where an identifier's payload starts or how its case folds
the object-name segment of every sharded path is the identifier's key form
the SDK read answers with the DISPLAY form the tree states rather than echoing the caller's spelling back
checks that a published tree states the key form in its paths and the display form in its bodies

client.why: computes the query's payload in a tab, to match a shard's entries against it — the browser half of §5's `the client computes the shard path directly`
key-forms every identifier it turns into a route, which is the residual that made a display-form URL out of a body-carried identifier
canonicalises a hex query to the form the published index and object names are keyed by

sweeps.why: who derives a §5 HASH INDEX KEY. This sweep did not exist while the index was hex-only, because there was nothing per-encoding to derive: `hashPrefix` took one string and a constant said it was hex. Now the producer keys from the chain's declared encoding and the client keys from the query's SHAPE, and the two have to meet on one shard — so the set of files that may compute an index key is as load-bearing as the set that may compute a shard PATH, and is swept the same way.

src.why: reads the `shapes` and `alphabet` rules out of the shared file and answers over them — the recognition rule and the refusal both live here, so neither is a table in a consumer
the codec: `hashPrefix` is the shard key and `identifierIndexKey` is what every entry is stored and compared under
a producer — keys its own generation-scoped index from the declaration it publishes, so it cannot declare one encoding and key another

reproduces the CLIENT's computation to check coverage, which is why it keys through `hashPrefix` here while quoting references verbatim everywhere else (see the exemption block above `checkTransaction`)

client.why: §2's classification, which became a DERIVATION SITE when the index started keying per shape: `shapesOf` decides whether a query reaches the index and `indexProbesOf` decides which shardS it computes — PLURAL, because one query can be admissible under two rows with two payloads and the client fetches both (§5.6). A row it declines to recognise, or a reading it drops, is a false absence under §5.0a and not a missing feature.
the browser half — computes the shard path in a tab from the query alone, which is the whole of §5's `the client computes the shard path directly`
the GLOBAL index's one writer: the only place that has seen every chain, and the only place that may write `/idx/hash/**`

present.why: FORMAT 1's DECODED-BYTE UNIT, AND THE ONLY THING LEFT THAT KNOWS WHAT HEX IS. It is private and reachable only after `identifierIndexKey` has already refused anything the `hex` alphabet does not admit, which is what turned the replaced `hexToBytes`'s unhandled `parseHexInt` crash into a refusal that names the encoding, the identifier and the offending character. THE COUNT IS THE PIN: format 2 must not grow a decoded-byte path, because decoding is the one thing the client cannot do without knowing the chain.

…and the one encoding a FORMAT-1 shard can hold, NAMED rather than assumed. It was `HashIndexEncoding` and described the whole index; it now describes one of two published formats, because the index keys per identifier SHAPE and a shape is derivable from the query string alone (Search-And-Routing.md §5). A hex-shaped constant that still claimed to describe the index would be the assumption the rename removed.

THE ONE REMAINING FOLD IN THIS MODULE, COUNTED RATHER THAN FORBIDDEN, because it is not a normalisation of anybody's identifier: `bytesToHex` renders format-1's STORED BYTES back into hex, and lowercase hex IS that format's alphabet rather than a decision about case. Counting it is what stops a second appearing beside it.

the refusal, and every path that reaches the hex-pair parser. An entry keyed from a string its declared alphabet does not admit is a hit that navigates to a 404, which §5 forbids outright. THE COUNT WENT 5 -> 6 BECAUSE THE MUTANT FOUND THE GAP: format 1's arm called `hexUnits` directly while only format 2 keyed through here, so `just byte-identity-mutant` still killed the demo producer with `invalid hex integer: 0x` — the exact crash this step replaced.

THE HEX PARSER, STILL HERE AND NOW UNREACHABLE WITH A NON-HEX DIGIT. Format 1 stores decoded pairs, so it has to parse them — but the public `hexToBytes` that took any string is on the absent list, and the private `hexUnits` that replaced it runs only after `identifierIndexKey` has refused by name. The count is the pin: a SECOND `parseHexInt` would be a second place deciding what an identifier is, without the refusal in front of it.

absent.why: GONE, not kept as a wrapper. It folded case unconditionally for every encoding — right for hex, destroys base58 and base64url — and a correctly-named hex-assuming entry point one identifier away from every call site is reachable by habit and indistinguishable from a choice in a diff.

GONE, for the same reason and with more force. It was PUBLIC, took any string, and reached `parseHexInt` on it — so four of the eight members of the closed set had no representation in the index at all, and anything it could not parse KILLED the producer with an unhandled ValueError naming a string function. `identifierIndexKey` refuses by name instead, and `hexUnits` above is private.

present.why: the two literal `0x` filters over published directory ENTRIES. These enumerate the tree the hash index keys, so they genuinely follow the index: a filter widened ahead of the index would enumerate a non-hex chain's entities and then fail to key them, which is worse than not seeing them.

the three former derivation sites, now enumerations. THE COUNT IS THE PIN: a fourth sharded path in this file either adds a fourth call here — which moves this number — or open-codes a slice, which the `absent` list below refuses. Before this, both halves counted only the `0x` filters, so a fourth `slice(2, 6)` was invisible to both.

absent.why: the open-coded hex shard rule, at three sites, building `/d/{chain}/tx/{shard}/`, `/d/{chain}/ts/{tsv}/{shard}/` and `/d/{chain}/g/{gen}/addr/{shard}/`. It DERIVED rather than enumerated, so the 'it follows the index' defence never covered it; it was also stricter than the function it duplicated, with neither the strip-only-if-present quirk nor the right-padding.
the tooling reads what was published rather than the declaration behind it, which is why it needs no JavaScript reader of the closed set.
